messages:
elaine: Quick Q — when our CLI logs in on Windows, where is the token actually stored by default? I ran a script on a coworker's machine and couldn't find it in %APPDATA% or my usual keyring.

mason: By default the CLI tries the OS keyring first (Windows Credential Manager), then falls back to a file in the user config dir. Which version are you on?

elaine: 0.9.3. I think it said 'no keyring available' during login. Is there a way to force file storage so my automation (PowerShell task) can read it reliably?

oliver: 0.9.x had flaky keyring detection on some Win images. We added an env var in 0.10 to force file mode (REDWOOD_CLI_TOKEN_FILE). If you set that to a path the CLI will write/read the token there.

elaine: awesome — where is that documented? I didn't see it in the quickstart.

mason: Not surfaced in quickstart yet, sorry. Docs PR incoming. For now you can do:

```
# PowerShell example
$env:REDWOOD_CLI_TOKEN_FILE = "$Env:USERPROFILE\\.redwood\\token.json"
redwood login --non-interactive --token $env:CI_REPO_TOKEN
```

mason: The token file is plain JSON with an expiry and token_type. Treat it like a secret.

alex: Note: if you do this for CI, make sure the runner user has a locked-down folder and rotate tokens frequently. CI secrets + file caching = risk if left world-readable.

elaine: Good call. Any gotchas around streaming or retries when you use file mode vs keyring? My script pipes output to another process.

kavi: Behavior is identical for API calls. The only difference is how credentials are loaded on startup. But watch for races: two processes starting at once might try to refresh and overwrite the token file. We added a simple file lock in 0.10 to reduce that, but it's advisory on Windows.

elaine: Hmm ok. Is the lock implemented with a lockfile or Win32 mutex?

oliver: Lockfile with an atomic rename + small backoff loop. On Windows networked filesystems that can fail. If you expect parallel runners, prefer per-job ephemeral directories and set REDWOOD_CLI_TOKEN_FILE accordingly.

elaine: Nice. Last thing — can I configure the CLI to always use short-lived tokens (like 1h) for scripts? I want auto-expiry rather than manual rotation.

mason: Short-lived tokens are supported from the auth service; CLI just stores whatever token you provide. You can request a token with a shorter TTL via the dashboard or our token-issue API. For scripts you can implement a refresh wrapper that calls the token endpoint and writes to REDWOOD_CLI_TOKEN_FILE before running the main job.

elaine: Perfect — I'll try the env var approach and report back if we hit the race. thanks all :raised_hands:

ci-bot: Note: opened issue #4127 to add docs for REDWOOD_CLI_TOKEN_FILE and guidance for CI patterns. Link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/docs/issues/4127

mason: Thanks @elaine — ping me if you hit anything weird on Win images.
